chapters.title: Pin it before you touch it

scenes.say: A two hundred line function has no tests, and your manager says clean it up. By the end, you'll change it without breaking anything, then design a task a machine can grade.
Today you will do three things. Pin down legacy code with tests, then refactor it. Keep your tests fast and reliable. And write a verifier that cheats can't beat.
lines: Pin legacy code with tests, then refactor
Write a verifier cheats can't beat

scenes.title: Clean up code with no tests
scenes.statement: A 200-line function has no tests. Restructure it without changing what it does.
scenes.say: Here's the problem. A two hundred line function has no tests. Change it safely. For example, calc invoice, with zero tests. The goal: the same results, but cleaner code.

scenes.head: Three habits, one lesson
scenes.say: Interviewers ask this to see whether you rewrite and hope, or work like a surgeon. Three habits answer it. First, pin today's behavior before you touch anything. Second, keep tests fast and trustworthy. Third, write a verifier that nobody can fool.

scenes.head: Renovating a house you live in
scenes.say: Think of renovating a house you live in. First, photograph every room. Then move one wall. Then compare with the photos. In code, the photos are tests.

scenes.head: Run it, write down what comes back
scenes.say: Here's a short stand in for your two hundred line monster. It adds tax, takes ten percent off for gold customers, and adds shipping under fifty. Don't hunt for bugs yet. Run it and record. Zero gives four ninety nine. One gives six oh seven. Ninety nine ninety nine gives one oh seven ninety nine.
Your turn. The recording says an empty invoice costs four ninety nine. That smells like a bug. Before you refactor, what do you do? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `calc_invoice(0)` returns 4.99, a probable bug. Before refactoring, you...

scenes.head: Freeze today's answers as asserts
scenes.say: Pin it as is. These are characterization tests: they describe today, bugs included. So no refactor can change anything by accident. The bug gets fixed later, in its own commit. Four asserts, one for gold. Run them. Pinned. Now you're allowed to touch the code.

panels.code:
assert calc_invoice(0) == 4.99
assert calc_invoice(1) == 6.07
assert calc_invoice(99.99) == 107.99
assert calc_invoice(99.99, True) == 97.19
print("pinned")

scenes.title: Is my tiny step safe?
scenes.statement: You change one line while refactoring. How do you learn in seconds that nothing else changed?
scenes.say: Here's the problem. You change one line. Did anything else change? For example, a typo in a tax helper. The goal: a red test, right away.

scenes.head: The safe loop
scenes.say: Now the loop. Make one tiny change, like extracting a helper. Run the tests, which takes seconds. Green? Commit. Red? Undo just that step, so a failure points at exactly one change.

scenes.head: Extract the tax step
scenes.say: Say you extract the tax step into its own helper. Your finger slips, and one point oh eight becomes one point eight. The code still runs, and the typo is easy to miss.
Your pinned tests run in order: zero, one, ninety nine ninety nine. Which assert fails first? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: With the `1.8` typo, which pinned call fails first?

scenes.head: Zero hides the typo
scenes.say: Call one fails. Zero times anything is still zero, so the zero test passed and hid the typo. One gives six seventy nine, not six oh seven. Ninety nine ninety nine gives a hundred seventy nine ninety eight. Red, so you undo that one step. Pick varied inputs.

scenes.head: Three temptations, three habits
scenes.say: Three temptations. Spot a bug mid refactor? Fix it in its own commit. Can't test it at all? Find a seam, a spot to inject a dependency. Tempted to rewrite from scratch? Don't. Take steps small enough to undo with one revert.
rows: Note it; fix in its own commit
Find a seam: a spot to pass in a fake
Steps small enough for one revert

scenes.title: Why does a test fail at midnight?
scenes.statement: A test passes all day and fails once at midnight. Make the whole suite fast and reliable.

example.input: a test that reads the real clock

scenes.say: Here's the problem. A test passes all day and fails once at midnight. For example, a test that reads the real clock. The goal: the same result on every run, on every machine.

scenes.head: The test pyramid
scenes.say: Three kinds of test, and why one flakes. Think of building a car. First, check each bolt alone. That's a unit test: one function, milliseconds, no database. Many of them, about seventy percent. Next, engine and gearbox on a bench: integration, about twenty. Last, test drive the whole car: end to end, slow, about ten.

scenes.head: Flaky? Pass the clock in
scenes.say: A flaky test passes sometimes, fails sometimes. Say yours fails only at midnight. The cause is hidden input: the real clock. Random numbers and the network do it too. Fix it by passing time in. Now a hundred is expired, ninety nine is not, every run.

scenes.head: A mock stands in for slow things
scenes.say: A mock replaces something slow or outside your control, like an email service. The test hands checkout a stand-in mailer, so no email is sent. It checks the return value, fifty, and that send was called once with receipt. A fake is a simple working copy, like an in-memory mailer. A mock only records calls.

panels.code:
from unittest.mock import Mock
def checkout(mailer, total):
    mailer.send("receipt")
    return total

mailer = Mock()
assert checkout(mailer, 50) == 50
mailer.send.assert_called_once_with("receipt")
print("ok")

scenes.say: Your turn. Same test, but checkout has a bug and sends the receipt twice. What happens when you run it? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: The mock caught the double send
scenes.say: It fails. The mock recorded two calls, and assert called once refuses that. No email left the building, yet the bug got caught.

output.text:
Expected 'send' to be called once. Called 2 times.
Calls: [call('receipt'), call('receipt')].

scenes.head: Over-mocking proves nothing
scenes.say: Here's the classic mistake. This test mocks the cart, tells the mock to return fifty, then asserts the mock returns fifty. It passes. It tests the mock. Mock the slow edges, not the thing you test.

panels.label: bad
panels.code:
from unittest.mock import Mock

cart = Mock()
cart.total.return_value = 50
assert cart.total() == 50
print("passed")

scenes.head: Follow-ups you'll get
scenes.say: Follow ups. Why are tests flaky? Clock, randomness, network, shared state. Is a hundred percent coverage good? No, it only shows lines ran. What do you test? Behavior and edge cases, not internals.
rows: No: it only shows lines ran
Behavior and edge cases, not internals

scenes.title: Grade code by machine
scenes.statement: Design a task a program can grade pass or fail, with no way to cheat.
scenes.say: Here's the problem. Design a task a program can grade, with no way to cheat. For example, merge overlapping intervals. This input must give this output, graded against a trusted reference on fifty seeded hidden cases.

scenes.head: A driving test
scenes.say: A verifier says pass or fail. Think of a driving test. The examiner follows a fixed checklist, the same for everyone. The route is a surprise, so you can't memorize it. And any good driver passes, not only one who drives exactly like the examiner.

scenes.head: Task: merge overlapping intervals
scenes.say: Our task: merge overlapping intervals. The spec says touching intervals merge, and output is sorted. The reference sorts, then extends the last interval or starts a new one. The sample gives one to six, eight to ten. And one to four, with four to five, becomes one to five.

scenes.head: A seed makes the cases repeatable
scenes.say: The generator takes a seed, a number that fixes the random generator. Seed zero always builds the same list, so a failure on seed thirty one reproduces on any machine, every run. Each case has zero to eight intervals, so the empty list is covered on purpose.

panels.code:
import random
def make_case(seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    case = []
    for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 8)):
        a = rng.randint(0, 20)
        case.append([a, a + rng.randint(1, 5)])
    return case
print(make_case(0)[:2], make_case(0) == make_case(0))

scenes.head: A solution that cheats
scenes.say: Now a cheater. It hard codes the sample. It passes the visible example. But hidden seeds it has never seen fail. Big inputs with a time limit catch slow solutions. And edge cases, like empty input, go in on purpose.

scenes.head: Fifty seeds, one verdict
scenes.say: The grader loops over fifty seeds, builds a case, and compares the candidate with the reference. It hands the candidate a copy, so it can't change the case. The real solution passes all fifty. The cheater fails on seed zero.
The cheater returns an empty list for anything but the sample. Out of the fifty hidden cases, how many does it pass? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: The cheater passes the sample. How does it do on the 50 hidden cases?

scenes.head: Passing by luck
scenes.say: Here's how many of the fifty cases each one passes. The real solution passes fifty. The cheater passes five, only the empty cases, where an empty answer is right.

scenes.head: Many right answers? Validate
scenes.say: Some problems accept many answers, like two sum with several valid pairs. Then don't compare with the reference output. Check the rules: two different indices, both in range, and the values add up to the target. Seven works with zero and two, or one and two. Both pass.

panels.code:
def check_pair(nums, t, out):
    i, j = out
    n = len(nums)
    if i == j or i not in range(n) or j not in range(n):
        return False
    return nums[i] + nums[j] == t
nums = [3, 3, 4, 6]
print(check_pair(nums, 7, [0, 2]), check_pair(nums, 7, [1, 2]))

scenes.head: Is the reference even right?
scenes.say: One more. Is the reference right? Compare it with a slow brute force on small inputs. Why seeds? Reproducible failures. Common mistake? A vague spec.
rows: Same tests every run, repro on demand

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Refactor legacy code safely? Pin behavior with characterization tests, then tiny steps. No tests, hard to test? Find a seam. Bug spotted midway? Note it, fix it in its own commit. Common mistake: rewriting from scratch.
rows: Pin behavior first, then tiny steps
Find a seam, inject, then add tests
Note it; fix in its own commit

scenes.say: Unit, integration, end to end? Many fast ones, few slow ones. Keep tests reliable? Pass in time and randomness. Mock or fake? A mock records calls, a fake is a simple working copy.
lines: Unit, integration, e2e: many fast, few slow.
Reliable: pass in time, randomness, I/O.
Mock records calls; fake is a working copy.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Design a verifier? Spec, reference, seeded hidden tests. Many valid answers? Validate the rules, don't compare text. How do you stop hard coding? Hidden cases, edge cases, time limits. Reference right? Cross check with brute force.

scenes.head: Practice this week
scenes.say: Try these three. Take any function you own and write four characterization tests before editing it. Find one test that reads the clock and pass the time in. Then write a seeded verifier for merge overlapping intervals, LeetCode fifty six, and run a cheater against it.
rows: 4 characterization tests on your own code
pin it before you touch it
Seeded verifier for LeetCode 56 · Merge Intervals

scenes.say: So say this. Pin behavior with tests, then take tiny steps. Keep tests deterministic, many unit tests and few end to end. And grade with a spec, a reference, and seeded hidden tests.
lines: Pin behavior first, then tiny steps.
Fast, deterministic tests: many unit, few end to end.
